segments.text: So, I don't use on milk, I don't use on milk, I usually tell patients to use the coconut milk or cream because it's the least processed of all the realms.
Okay guys, the ratio of actual healthcare professionals to random influencers online is already disappointingly low.
We cannot afford for our doctors to be spreading misinformation too.
But I'm Abby Sharp. I'm the internet's no BS dietitian. And while I guess I'm relieved she
isn't recommending raw milk, I am hugely disappointed in a doctor spewing misinformation
and food fear mongering. Let's break this down. Processing does not mean bad. This misinformed
belief is grounded in an appeal to nature's fallacy, when in fact, in many cases, some processing
can actually make a food healthier, more accessible or safer. In the context of non-dairy milk,
a lot of the options are fortified with bone-supporting nutrients like calcium and vitamin D
so that it can be more nutritionally comparable to dairy milk. Two, what kind of coconut milk
are we even talking about? Because while the classic kind of coconut milk or cream that you
find in the can is basically like water and coconut in most cases. The carton coconut beverage that
we find alongside other non-dairy milks is basically processed the exact same with emulsifiers,
gums, flavors, and added vitamins that we might see in almond or oat. Three, for the vast majority
people, the level of processing should not be the most important indicator of a healthy option.
we should be looking at how much protein it contains,
which spoiler alert, oat, almond, and coconut
all kind of suck in that department.
We should also be considering how many calories,
how much sugar, how much saturated fat is in that product,
which is what actually increases the risk
of chronic diseases like cancer.
Please, make it make sense.
And finally, not only does this post wrongfully insinuate
that almond and oat milk cause cancer,
which spoiler alert friends, they do not,
but it instead makes a recommendation for the milk
that provides the most calories
and the highest saturated fat content,
both of which are associated with an increased risk
of chronic disease, obesity, heart disease,
and yes, even some cancers.
Now, I'm certainly not saying that coconut milk
or coconut beverage causes cancer or chronic disease,
but I'm simply pointing out some factual gaps
in this fear-mongering storyline
that just do not add up.
Bottom line, friends, processing in non-dairy milk
does not cause cancer.
How a food is processed
shouldn't be the most important criteria
for a healthy choice,
and your choice in milk should come down
to what values are most important to you in a product,
whether that's the protein in soy,
the omega-3s in grass-fed dairy,
the minimal calories in almond,
or the fiber or flavor of oat.
I promise you, what you put in your coffee
will not make or break your health.
Next.
